concept.name: Slippage tolerance
concept.definition: Slippage tolerance is the maximum deviation a user accepts between the expected price of an on-chain swap and the price it actually executes at; if execution would exceed this bound, the transaction reverts.
concept.intuition: It is the 'don't fill me worse than X' dial on a DEX trade — your insurance against the price moving between signing and execution.
concept.mechanics: Price slippage is the gap between the quoted price when a swap is submitted and the realized execution price, caused by other trades landing first and by the trade's own price impact. Wallets/routers encode slippage tolerance as a minimum output amount; if the pool cannot deliver at least that much, the transaction fails (and only gas is lost).
concept.failure_modes: Setting tolerance too high invites sandwich attackers to push execution to the worst allowed price; too low, and transactions revert repeatedly in volatile markets, wasting gas without executing.
concept.misconceptions: Slippage tolerance does not reduce price impact — it only caps the damage you accept; the trade's own impact is computed by the AMM regardless. A failed, reverted swap still costs gas.
concept.example: Swapping 50,000 USDC for ETH quoted at 12.5 ETH with 0.5% slippage tolerance sets a minimum of 12.4375 ETH; if a sandwich bot moves the pool so you'd only get 12.3 ETH, the transaction reverts instead of filling.
